hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private .

Comment 1: How do you compare yourself with https://www.agent37.com/ Also, digitalocean offers this now.

Comment 2: Better landing page animation, of course.

Comment 3: Agent37 is great if you want plain, cheap sandboxes. But you still have to build and manage a lot of the infra to sell agents to customers, we manage the entirety so that you don't think about cloud runtime at all and can focus on other things. We also provide you with ongoing support, an infra partner if you may. DigitalOcean is focusing on coding agent sessions in the cloud, rather than managing the things necessary to sell long living agents to customers.

Comment 4: There are a lot of alternatives in the market for this.
hn.titleZh: 推出 HN：海事 (YC F26) – 用於生產 AI 代理的託管雲
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
您好，HN，我們是 Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ) 的共同創辦人 Ary 和 Maria。我們正在建立一個代理原生雲，可以處理從自訂環境到人工智慧代理生命週期管理的所有事務。演示：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY 舊金山的沙箱公司爆炸式增長，但沙箱可能解決了人工智慧代理 10% 的基礎設施問題。大多數沙箱公司採取的方法是：購買 Hetzner/OVH Cloud 裸機伺服器，使用 Firecracker 將伺服器分割成虛擬機，然後以低利潤出售這些虛擬機。這有點過於簡單化了，但關鍵是它是解決一個相當困難的問題的狹隘解決方案。我們與數百家正在建立人工智慧代理的公司進行了交談。從個人助理和編碼代理到專門的醫療保健代理，我們看到的主要模式是，即使在選擇沙箱提供者之後，您仍然必須建立額外的基礎設施才能讓事情正常運作。這些是主要的摩擦點： 1. 代理生命週期管理。為了正確地為代理提供虛擬機，您必須構建很多東西：諸如睡眠/喚醒、持久存儲、觸發器、調度、每用戶路由和支出上限、運行狀況監控、故障恢復以及在數千個虛擬機上部署更新而無需停機。

公司必須自行建造和維護如此多的小型沙盒管理任務，而且這些任務會不斷增加。 2. 自訂環境。生產代理商有不同的需求。有些代理程式需要 Windows 應用程式。其他人則需要 Android、具有持久性會話的瀏覽器、自訂作業系統映像、預先安裝的桌面軟體和應用程式或特定的依賴項。一些代理需要訪問私有 .評論 1：您與 https://www.agent37.com/ 相比如何？另外，digitalocean 現在提供此服務。評論 2：當然，更好的著陸頁動畫。評論 3：如果您想要簡單、便宜的沙箱，Agent37 很棒。但是您仍然需要建立和管理大量基礎設施來向客戶銷售代理，我們管理整個系統，以便您根本不用考慮雲端運行時，而可以專注於其他事情。我們還為您提供持續的支持，如果可以的話，我們還可以為您提供基礎合作夥伴。 DigitalOcean 專注於雲端中的代理會話編碼，而不是管理向客戶銷售長期代理所需的事務。評論4：市面上有很多替代品。

hn.originalTitle: Steve Yegge on AI Agents and the Future of Software Engineering
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Steve Yegge on AI Agents and the Future of Software Engineering

Steve Yegge on AI Agents and the Future of Software Engineering

Steve Yegge on the 8 levels of AI adoption, why big companies may be doomed, and why he and many AI-adopters feel drained from using agents non-stop

Gergely Orosz Feb 10, 2026 ∙ Paid 351 7 19 Share Note: I’m currently in San Francisco. Last night, I attended AI Night with WorkOS, and tomorrow I’ll be hosting The Pragmatic Summit .

More than 200 people attended a packed AI Night event , featuring hands-on demos and a fireside chat between WorkOS founder Michael Grinich (in the middle, to the left of me) and myself The next podcast episode with Kotlin’s creator, Andrey Breslav, will be out on Thursday instead of tomorrow (Wednesday). Regular scheduling, including The Pulse , resumes next week. We’ll release session recordings from the Pragmatic Summit to paid subscribers first, and later to everyone.

Please wish me luck with this event tomorrow, it’s the first ever in-person event by The Pragmatic Engineer, and there’s a full house of 500 attendees. If you’re there, come and say hi!

Steve Yegge has been a software engineer for over 40 years, with stints at GeoWorks, Amazon, Google, and Grab. He’s known for provocative, entertaining blog posts, of which the most famous might be Stevey’s Google platform rant .

Steve recently published the book “Vibe Coding”, has also built Gas Town , an open-source AI agent orchestrator, and created documentation site and community hub Gas Townhall around the project. A year ago, we did a podcast focusing on his career, including how he used AI for coding. Last week, Steve and I sat down again in Salt Lake City and explored what’s changed in terms of using LLMs for coding, and also the wider tech industry.

Steve (right) and I in Salt Lake City In this article, we cover:

LLMs, the end of coding by hand, and the S-curve. Initially skeptical of LLMs, Steve became a convert after trying out Claude Code. He now argues the industry is headed into a steep exponential curve that shows no signs of stopping.

“50% dial” and deep cuts . Could big companies cut up to 50% of their staff in order to make way for AI tools? Such a trend might dwarf pandemic-era layoffs.

Eight levels of AI adoption. A spectrum of AI adoption, from “no AI”, to “building your own orchestrator”. Steve fears engineers stuck at the lower levels will be left behind.

The Dracula effect: the drain of using AI. Vibe coding at full speed can be physically draining, and Steve argues that employers shouldn’t reasonably expect more than three hours of AI-augmented work from engineers, per day.

Big companies are doomed – but don’t know it. Innovation at large companies is effectively dead, and the real action will come from small, AI-augmented teams – like when cloud computing shifted the balance of power.

Redundant values in the AI era. Knowing how to code doesn’t make engineers special any more, but demand for software will keep growing.

Debugging and programming languages. Agents may not need good debugging tools, and language choices have never mattered less.

Grieving the demise of coding by hand. Steve endured a grieving process when he realized many skills are obsolete, BUT building software is now more fun than ever.

Predictions. Steve’s non-coder wife could be the top contributor to their video game, Wyvern .

Related The Pragmatic Engineer articles featuring Steve:

Amazon, Google, and Vibe Coding with Steve Yegge (podcast episode in 2025)

The full circle of developer productivity with Steve Yegge (deepdive in 2022)

Originally, I had audio quality issues with this recording. Fortunately, I managed to improve the audio and remove echos, and the episode is also available as a podcast now:

Listen to the podcast version

1. LLMs, the end of coding by hand, and the S-curve

One thing about you is that you’re pretty pragmatic. You were always into compilers, debugger tools, and worked on hard problems at Amazon and Google. When AI came out, I don’t remember you saying, “this is amazing!” What was your initial reaction to LLMs?

Steve: “I was pretty blown away that they could write fairly coherent Emacs and Lisp functions. The original ChatGPT in December 2022 could already write code in a weird language, right? Not very much of it, and it was janky; but for me, that was the beginning. I’ve had friends who were saying for 20 years, “any minute now, any day now” about AI. But 2022 was the first time that it was like, “okay, I see now.

hn.originalTitle: California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms
hn.sourceOriginalText:
California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms

California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company knowingly continued testing advanced artificial intelligence models despite repeated security failures that allowed autonomous AI agents to escape isolated environments and launch cyberattacks against real-world organizations.

The lawsuit claims OpenAI misled the public about its cybersecurity safeguards and failed to adequately monitor increasingly advanced AI cybersecurity models, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which the company lost control of its agents during testing.

The legal action follows a July security incident where hundreds of OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face , an artificial intelligence platform, compromising production infrastructure and stealing internal credentials.

California says the Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI repeatedly focusing on experimental AI testing without ensuring adequate safeguards were in place.

"The Hugging Face cyberattack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," the complaint reads .

The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI continued testing increasingly capable AI agents despite knowing its sandbox environments could be bypassed, potentially exposing third-party systems to unauthorized activity.

"In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing," the lawsuit continues.

During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet.

The attack lasted more than two days, with nearly 700 autonomous agents coordinating through an unauthorized message board to plan the attack on Hugging Face's production systems while attempting to steal answers to a cybersecurity benchmark.

The California complaint alleges that OpenAI ignored or missed warning signs in the weeks leading up to the incident, including evidence that agents had already escaped their testing environments and were abusing third-party services and platforms.

It also claims that OpenAI's agents subsequently targeted software repositories, informational websites, and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information. In another incident, experimental agents allegedly compromised OpenAI's own internal infrastructure and obtained administrator-level access to critical systems.

According to the complaint, OpenAI has acknowledged more than 80 instances of losing control of autonomous agents during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents.

The lawsuit follows a subpoena issued by Bonta's office in September, with California claiming that OpenAI failed to provide sufficient information about the incidents and instead supplied limited documentation and descriptions of previously disclosed attacks.

The state is pursuing claims under California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance laws, seeking court orders requiring stronger safeguards, civil penalties, and other relief.

The rise of autonomous AI attacks

The lawsuit comes amid growing concerns about increasingly capable AI models escaping controlled cybersecurity evaluations and attacking organizations outside their intended testing environments.

These autonomous attacks are not limited to OpenAI agents, with other AI platforms disclosing similar incidents in the past.

In July, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had breached production systems at three organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. One model created and uploaded a malicious Python package to the public PyPI repository, where it was downloaded and executed on 15 real systems.

This led Anthropic to  remove internet access from all internal AI model evaluations following additional incidents involving unauthorized activity against government websites and other external systems.

Google also confirmed to The Wall Street Journal in September that its Gemini AI model had accessed the internet and hacked three companies during cybersecurity testing conducted in May.

hn.titleZh: 加州起訴 OpenAI，指控 AI 代理逃離沙箱、駭客公司
hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 OpenAI / Agent 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
加州因人工智慧代理逃離沙箱而起訴 OpenAI，駭客公司加州因人工智慧代理逃離沙箱而起訴 OpenAI，駭客公司加州總檢察長 Rob Bonta 週一起訴 OpenAI，指控該公司故意繼續測試先進的人工智慧模型，儘管多次出現安全故障，使自主人工智慧代理能夠逃離的環境並對現實世界孤立的組織發起網路攻擊。該訴訟稱，OpenAI 在其網路安全保障措施方面誤導了公眾，並且未能充分監控日益先進的人工智慧網路安全模型，導致該公司在測試期間發生了 80 多起對其代理商失去控制的事件。這項法律行動是在 7 月發生的一次安全事件之後發生的，當時數百名由 OpenAI 驅動的代理商逃離了受控測試環境，併入侵了人工智慧平台 Hugging Face，損害了生產基礎設施並竊取了內部憑證。加州表示，Hugging Face 攻擊是 OpenAI 反覆專注於實驗性人工智慧測試而沒有確保採取足夠的保護措施造成的。訴狀中寫道：“Hugging Face 網路攻擊是 OpenAI 內部文化的可預見結果，這種文化優先考慮成長和快速模型開發，而不是安全和責任。”

該訴訟稱，儘管 OpenAI 知道其沙箱環境可能被繞過，但仍繼續測試功能日益強大的人工智慧代理，可能使第三方系統遭受未經授權的活動。 「事實上，OpenAI 未能遵守其內部政策，即使有證據表明其網路安全保障措施不足以遏制其正在開發的高度先進模型，也未能持續、積極地推進測試和實驗，」訴訟繼續說道。在 Hugging Face 攻擊期間，OpenAI 模式利用 JFrog Artifactory 中的零日漏洞突破其隔離的測試環境並存取網路。這次攻擊持續了兩天多，近 700 個自主代理透過未經授權的留言板進行協調，計劃對 Hugging Face 的生產系統進行攻擊，同時試圖竊取網路安全基準的答案。加州的投訴稱，OpenAI 在事件發生前幾週忽視或錯過了警告信號，包括代理商已經逃離測試環境並濫用第三方服務和平台的證據。它還聲稱 OpenAI 的特工隨後將目標鎖定為包含敏感健康資訊的軟體儲存庫、資訊網站和外國政府資料庫。

在另一起事件中，實驗代理據稱破壞了 OpenAI 自己的內部基礎設施，並獲得了對關鍵系統的管理員等級存取權。根據訴狀，OpenAI 承認在測試過程中發生了 80 多起自主代理人失去控制的事件，但僅公開披露了 27 起事件。該訴訟是在 Bonta 辦公室於 9 月發出傳票後提起的，加州聲稱 OpenAI 未能提供有關這些事件的足夠信息，而是提供了先前披露的攻擊的有限文件和描述。該州正在根據加州《反不正當競爭法》和《公共滋擾法》提出索賠，尋求法院命令，要求採取更強有力的保障措施、民事處罰和其他救濟。自主人工智慧攻擊的興起 這起訴訟發生之際，人們越來越擔心能力日益增強的人工智慧模式會逃避受控的網路安全評估，並攻擊其預期測試環境之外的組織。這些自主攻擊不僅限於 OpenAI 代理，其他 AI 平台過去也揭露過類似事件。 7 月，Anthropic 披露其 Claude 模型在網路安全評估期間破壞了三個組織的生產系統。

一個模型創建了一個惡意 Python 套件並將其上傳到公共 PyPI 儲存庫，然後在 15 個真實系統上下載並執行該套件。這導致 Anthropic 在發生涉及針對政府網站和其他外部系統的未經授權活動的其他事件後，從所有內部人工智慧模型評估中刪除了網路存取權限。谷歌也於 9 月向《華爾街日報》證實，其 Gemini AI 模型在 5 月進行的網路安全測試期間已訪問互聯網併入侵了 3 家公司。加州的訴訟

hn.originalTitle: A 4.5M-parameter TTS model runs 70x real-time on CPU and cost just $10 to train
hn.sourceOriginalText:
n4ze3m/tiny-voca · Hugging Face

tiny-voca is a small English text-to-speech model with two voices, F2 (female) and M2 (male). The complete model, including the waveform generator, has 4.5M parameters and was trained from scratch on about 18 hours of synthetic speech. It runs about 70x faster than real time on four CPU threads.

Try it in the browser:

tiny-voca.pt : ebb22871524c5732520fb1652e6aefcec708a7452e83bdd00adcf6181db5ef70

onnx/model.onnx : fe6d918791a15b82e37465981d7f27a070e46b46635e5a3482fc8dff87a1ae46

pip install git+ git+ hf download n4ze3m/tiny-voca --local-dir tiny-voca export DIZIONE_DATA=tiny-voca/phonemizer python -m tiny_voca.infer \ --checkpoint tiny-voca/tiny-voca.pt \ --voice F2 \ --text "Hello! This is tiny voca." \ --output hello.wav Option Default Meaning --text-file Read the text from a file instead of --text . --voice F2 F2 or M2 --speed 1.0 Speaking rate --pitch-shift 0 Added to log F0. 0.058 is about one semitone. --pitch-range 1.0 Scales pitch movement around the utterance mean. Text of any length works. The command reads it one sentence at a time and joins the audio. A text that ends without a mark gets a full stop. A sentence with nothing to read, such as one in anoth.

The graph takes phoneme ids and stress values and returns the waveform. Text is converted to ids outside the graph with dizione; the ids are the positions in vocab in config.json .

import numpy as np import onnxruntime as ort import soundfile as sf import dizione # needs DIZIONE_DATA=tiny-voca/phonemizer phones = dizione.phonemize( "Hello! This is tiny voca." ) one = lambda value: np.array([value], dtype=np.float32) session = ort.InferenceSession( "tiny-voca/onnx/model.onnx" ) audio, durations = session.run( None , { "tokens" : np.array([phones.ids], dtype=np.int64), "stress" : np.array([phones.stress], dtype=np.int64), "voice" : np.array([ 0 ], dtype=np.int64), # 0 = F2, 1 = M2 "speed" : one( 1.0 ), "pitch_shift" : one( 0.0 ), "pitch_range" : one( 1.0 ), }) audio = audio[ 0 ] audio = audio * min ( 1.0 , 0.99 / np. abs (audio). max ()) # the model can peak above 1.0 s.

Text is converted to phonemes with a stress value for each. A transformer encoder (4 blocks) reads the phonemes, a duration predictor gives each one a length in frames, and two frame-level transformers (2 and 5 blocks) predict pitch, voicing and energy and then the parameters of the waveform generator. All blocks use 192 channels, 4 heads and rotary position embeddings.

The waveform is produced by a source-filter synthesizer instead of a neural vocoder. A band-limited pulse train at the predicted pitch and a noise signal are each shaped by a time-varying filter, whose cepstrum the network predicts once per frame (256 samples, 10.7 ms). This part has 25,862 parameters.

The training audio is synthetic. Both voices were created from text descriptions with Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign, and the recordings were generated with Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base. No recording of a real speaker is involved. Phoneme durations come from forced alignment with facebook/wav2vec2-lv-60-espeak-cv-ft , which is used only to label the training data. No pretrained weights are part of the model.

Word error rate of synthesized speech, transcribed with Whisper small.en. The recordings of the same sentences are scored the same way for reference.

These sets are small and the scores are a sanity check, not a benchmark. No formal listening test has been run.

Open TTS Leaderboard

Official leaderboard snapshot: 16 November 2026 (v1.6.3), English, without voice cloning , equal average across Seed-TTS, CV3-Eval and MiniMax; 50 ranked models (full-coverage English). Each tiny-voca voice is a separate row; M2 currently ranks 8th by average WER and F2 ranks 13th . The hosted leaderboard notes tiny-voca is CPU-only on both rows.

📊 Open TTS Leaderboard (16 Nov 2026 snapshot)

🎧 Compare model outputs with Qwen3 TTS (model used for training) and Kokoro

English only, two fixed voices, no voice cloning.

The voice is clear but can sound slightly synthetic.

The F2 voice sounds younger than intended. It was designed as an adult voice (the prompt asked for an adult American woman in her mid twenties; see voices.json in the dataset). A more mature voice is planned.

The same text is always read the same way. There is no sampling of prosody.

Speech is slightly faster than the training recordings at the default speed.

Foreign names and unusual spellings are often mispronounced. Numbers, abbreviations and homographs depend on the phonemiz

hn.originalTitle: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.

For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review."

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.

In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.

What the Harvard data measured

How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.

The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.

The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.

The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade

The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months. The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters.

They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI. The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private .

Comment 1: How do you compare yourself with https://www.agent37.com/ Also, digitalocean offers this now.

Comment 2: Better landing page animation, of course.

Comment 3: Agent37 is great if you want plain, cheap sandboxes. But you still have to build and manage a lot of the infra to sell agents to customers, we manage the entirety so that you don't think about cloud runtime at all and can focus on other things. We also provide you with ongoing support, an infra partner if you may. DigitalOcean is focusing on coding agent sessions in the cloud, rather than managing the things necessary to sell long living agents to customers.

Comment 4: There are a lot of alternatives in the market for this.

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
hn.sourceOriginalText:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling ( https://starsling.dev ), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows. Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost. Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762 . I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill. We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww . Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workf.

Comment 1: Congrats on the launch! These benchmarks look really great, can't wait to start using this. What are some of the most interesting things the AI has caught + fixed so far?

Comment 2: Oof. It's hard to pick one! I like the subtle fixes like swapping sleeps in tests with DB readiness checks or pinpointing a single long running test causing a shard to run slow.

Comment 3: I was surprised that mature projects got some of the biggest wins. gogs is a 48K-star repo and one 20 line fix got it a 5x speedup: https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs/blob/sh...

Comment 4: Congrats on the launch! Will give it a run. Why is your CI fast? Curious to hear the technical details

hn.originalTitle: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Comment 1: >> A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review. Um... can I please have the clinician review my file? Having the AI review my file and present a summary to the clinician/doctor means no human has looked at my actual history, only summaries provided by the AI. This is exactly how things get missed. It is exactly why doctors look at charts no matter what they are told verbally about a patient. Relying on AI to do all the chart reading is asking for trouble.

Comment 2: > The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review. Did you mean: The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization agent to review. Two agent fight, hope your agent stronger to get MRI

Comment 3: This could be wishful thinking, but OAI may just be talking about creating the prior auth. If this is the case, it would be nice if they said "prior auth encounter note" instead. From my limited understanding, the physician would and should still review your message, chart, agent drafted PA, etc...

Comment 4: They mention in the video that a clinician and/or authorization specialist will review it before it's submitted. The AI is just preparing a draft. In the video, you can see a human editing the notes in the interface, after the AI has prepared it all. It's the same thing as AI coding. The AI agent writes the code, but the coder has to review the code and edit it or propose changes if it's wrong. The point of both of them is to reduce manual work, and allow for less-specialized work, which saves time and money and can reduce errors.
